extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, breeders, and students/readers of evolutionary biology/natural history
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing secondary sexual characters in quadrupeds (mammals) — how to tell whether a structure or behaviour is a product of sexual selection, its likely function (offence, defence, attraction), its mode and timing of development, and supporting observational evidence (including domesticated animals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Late-life acquisition and sex-limited transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters which have acquired these characteristic qualities, occurred rather late in life, and were consequently to a large extent limited in their transmission to the same sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a trait appears only late in ontogeny and mainly in one sex, this timing helps explain why it is often transmitted primarily to that same sex (examples: size differences in Scotch deer-hounds where males reach full size later than females). Consider development timing when inferring inheritance patterns and sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male organs developed as means of defence against other males
rubrics_metrics.description: The males of some few quadrupeds possess organs or parts developed solely as a means of defence against the attacks of other males.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether structures (horns, tusks, shields, manes) are used in male–male combat; if so, sexual selection via male–male competition is indicated (examples: deer using upper horn branches; Oryx fencing; rhinoceroses parrying blows; boar shield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Morphology and age-related change indicate offensive vs defensive function
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in the form of weapons with age (or between jaws) can indicate whether they serve for offence or defence; e.g., lower tusks used for fighting in prime boars but curved upper tusks in old age serve chiefly for defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ontogenetic and morphological details (which tusks/horns are sharp/projecting, curvature with age, which side/position impacts combat) to infer function; compare related species and fossil records for timing of development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural hair (manes, ruffs) can serve as protection in fights
rubrics_metrics.description: The mane of the lion forms a good defence against the attacks of rival lions; broad ruff in Canadian lynx, stallion manes, and thick bison manes may protect neck/head during male–male combat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe fighting behaviour (do rivals seize the nape/neck?) and whether hair is more developed in males; but beware: protective function may not be original cause of development — require behavioural corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female mate choice (females select partners) as evidence for sexual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the female prefers any particular male... the female selects her partner; it would be a strange anomaly if female quadrupeds... did not generally, or at least often, exert some choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for direct/indirect evidence of female choice (e.g., females returning to familiar males, escaping during male fights to pair with a chosen male, documented preferences in wild and captive observations). Female choice supports sexual selection via female preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic-animal observations of mate preferences (size, familiarity, colour, individual characters)
rubrics_metrics.description: With most of our domesticated quadrupeds, strong individual antipathies and preferences are frequently exhibited, and much more commonly by the female than by the male... females often influenced by size, bright colour, and individual characters, as well as by previous familiarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use well-documented breeder/veterinarian observations and reliable anecdotes (dogs, horses, cattle, pigs) as evidence for preferences; consider familiarity, size, and conspicuous traits as candidate female preferences when inferring sexual selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male vocal enlargement/usage during the breeding-season may be sexually selected
rubrics_metrics.description: Almost all male animals use their voices much more during the rutting-season... the throats (larynx and thyroid bodies) of stags periodically become enlarged at the beginning of the breeding-season.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess seasonal enlargement/use of vocal organs and whether calls function to challenge rivals, attract females, or both. Consider species-specific evidence (gibbons' octave, laryngeal sacks in gorillas/orangs, Mycetes caraya choruses). Distinguish between mere nervous-excitement vocalisation and signals used in mate competition/attraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Odour and scent-glands often linked to reproduction and sexual attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: In other species the glands are confined to the males, or are more developed than in the females; and they almost always become more active during the rutting-season... the odour emitted must be of considerable importance to the male.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the presence, sexual dimorphism, seasonal activity, muscular control, and anatomical complexity of scent organs (elephant side-face glands, musk-sack of musk-deer, suborbital pits). Such features suggest a role in exciting or alluring females; use castration/age data where available to test reproductive linkage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long-continued use may produce inherited effects (use-inheritance alternative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The frequent use of the voice, under the strong excitement of love, jealousy, and rage, continued during many generations, may at last have produced an inherited effect on the vocal organs...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing origin of a trait, weigh two possibilities: direct sexual selection (preference or competition) versus inherited enlargement from habitual use. Seek evidence distinguishing them (e.g., development in young, heritability experiments, anatomical specializations beyond mere use).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual dimorphism in hair (beards, crests, dewlaps, manes) as candidate sexual-selection traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Male quadrupeds of many kinds differ from the females in having more hair, or hair of a different character, on certain parts of their faces... beards, whiskers, manes, crests, and dewlaps are often much more developed in the male.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document sexual differences in hair distribution/texture and seasonal appearance; consider whether these serve in combat protection, display, or are incidental. Use keeper/breeder reports, castration effects, and observations of fighting or display to infer function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution: presence of a sexual difference does not prove original adaptive function
rubrics_metrics.description: It does not, however, follow... that when the hair on the neck serves as a defence, that it was originally developed for this purpose... it is not probable that these hairs were specially developed for this purpose; otherwise the young and the females would have been equally protected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume current utility equals historical origin. Consider alternative explanations (correlated variation, seasonal expression, age-limited development). Look for supporting evidence such as sex-limited inheritance, castration effects, and whether juveniles/females share the trait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seasonality and castration tests as indicators of reproductive function
rubrics_metrics.description: They (glands/hair/odour) almost always become more active during the rutting-season... their development is checked by castration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use seasonality (breeding-season enlargement/activity) and effects of castration or age to test whether a structure is tied to reproductive function/sexual selection. If trait disappears or fails to develop after castration, this supports reproductive/sexual-selection linkage.
